What is a Copy.ai workflow?

A workflow connects actions so the output of one step can inform the next. A simple example starts with a company name and public website, collects relevant facts and turns those facts into a short briefing note. The next step might draft a message for review. The useful part is the connection between the research and the draft, because the writer can see which information the message should use.

Define the result before building the workflow. An account brief might need the company’s industry, an approved product description and a few relevant public facts. A campaign draft might need an audience, a product benefit and a link. Give each stage the information it needs and keep a clear review point before anyone sends or publishes the output.

Map a repeatable task in plain language

Imagine a small agency offers website maintenance to independent shops. The team wants to prepare an internal brief about each shop before deciding whether its services fit. Start with the public site and the agency’s approved service details. The first step collects the relevant public information. The second organizes it into a short note. The third proposes questions a team member can review before writing a message.

Keep the first version narrow. If you include several source types, multiple audiences and several outputs at once, it becomes hard to tell where a mistake came from. Test the workflow with one example you already know well. Confirm that the results use the correct business and that important facts can be traced to the source. Add more steps after the basic process works.

Choose inputs that make the result predictable

For each input, describe what it should contain. A company name may be ambiguous, so include the correct public website where available. A product description should come from approved source material. If the workflow needs a region or language, collect it directly rather than asking the model to infer it from a name.

Decide what should happen if a required field is missing. For example, a brief can say that a fact could not be verified and leave the draft for review. It is more useful to surface a missing detail than to produce confident wording based on a guess. Write down the expected format so the next person can understand the input requirements.

Research with a clear source trail

Research steps work best when the goal is specific. A team may want to understand what a business sells, who it serves or which public pages explain its services. Define the scope before collecting information. Keep links to the pages that support each important point. A source trail helps the reviewer check whether a statement applies to the right business and whether it is current.

Separate verified facts from possible opportunities. An online shop might publicly list its product categories. That does not establish what its owner wants to change next. If the workflow identifies a possible improvement, describe it as an observation to review rather than a confirmed need. This keeps the next stage grounded in what the research actually found.

Review results for outdated or unrelated information

A search result can refer to an old page or a business with the same name. Verify the site, date and context of each important result. Compare it with the current public information. If you cannot confirm a detail, remove it or mark it for follow-up. This matters for sales content, where a specific but wrong reference can undermine trust.

Keep the research summary short enough to check. Use a small number of fields that help the reviewer make a decision. A long report full of background details may slow the process. Include the facts that support the draft and the questions that still need a human answer. Save the source links with the summary so later revisions do not depend on memory.

Create go-to-market content from approved facts

Use the approved service description and the research note to create a draft that matches the intended audience. For the maintenance agency, the useful opening may be about managing seasonal updates or making it easier to keep product information current. Check that any observation refers to something the reviewer can confirm. Keep the proposed next step simple and relevant.

Different channels need different outputs. A landing page can explain the service and show what is included. An email draft may introduce one relevant benefit and propose a next step. A short internal note can help the team prepare a call. Use the same facts where they apply and adapt the level of detail to the channel.

Build a review step into the process

Give the reviewer the source, the generated draft and the intended destination. Ask them to check names, facts, claims and wording. A message should make sense to the person receiving it and should follow the team’s approval process. Keep the output as a draft until the appropriate person has reviewed it.

Set aside examples where the process went wrong. If it repeatedly picks the wrong business, require a website input. If it invents an outcome, require a source for any performance claim. If it produces generic copy, include a clearer audience and one approved example. Fix the cause in the workflow rather than correcting the same issue manually in every draft.

Test the workflow before scaling it

Run a few examples that represent the range of normal work. Include one straightforward case and one with missing information. Check whether the workflow handles both in a useful way. Review how long each stage takes and where a person still needs to make a decision. A workflow that consistently returns a short verified brief can be valuable even if the team writes the final message themselves.

Keep the test data limited to what the process needs. If the team handles private customer information, confirm where it can be used and who can see the results. For an initial trial, public company details and approved sample content can be enough. Check any integration permissions before connecting a business system or enabling actions beyond creating drafts.

Decide whether the offer fits your work

Choose one process and measure how long it takes today. Include searching for information, collecting links, writing a draft and getting review. Then run the same task with a workflow. Compare the time to a verified result and count the corrections needed. A useful process should make the work easier to repeat and the output easier to review.

For a small team, decide who owns the inputs and who approves the result. Document the source and format used at each stage. Keep an example of a good result for future tests. If the team changes its offer or audience, update the approved source and test a few outputs before relying on the new version.

Frequently asked questions

Can Copy.ai help with research?

A workflow can help organize information around a specific question. Define the sources and keep links with the results. Check the important details before using them in customer material. A focused research note can be easier to verify than a long draft that mixes facts and suggestions.

Can I use it to draft sales messages?

Use approved service details and relevant information about the intended audience. Ask for a draft that makes a clear, specific point. Review the facts, wording and destination before anyone sends it. For a customer campaign, keep the review and approval step in the process.

Do I need a large team to use a workflow?

A solo freelancer can use a small workflow to prepare notes or repeat a brief. Start with a task you already understand and a result you can check quickly. Expand the process when you can see that each extra step saves time or improves the result.

Example of a three-step research workflow

For the maintenance agency, the first action can collect the shop’s public home page and product categories. Limit the result to the business name, what it sells and the links that support those details. The second action can create a short internal note that connects the information to the agency’s approved services. Require the note to identify anything that needs checking. The last action can propose an opening line and a question for a team member to review.

Try the example with two businesses that have similar names. Check that each result uses the correct website. Then try a site with little public information. The useful response in that case is a short note about the missing details and a place for the reviewer to add verified information. Keep both cases as examples when revising the workflow.

If the draft is meant for a landing page instead, change the final output while keeping the verified source. Ask for a short heading, one useful example and a call to action. Compare it with the approved offer and check whether the next step is easy to find. This lets you test a different delivery format without repeating research.

Make approvals visible to the next person

When a workflow is shared, add a simple status field to the output. A brief could be ready for fact checking, ready for drafting or approved for its intended placement. Include the date of the source review and the name of the source document where appropriate. This helps a teammate tell whether the latest draft can be used or whether a product detail changed after the draft was prepared.

Review how the workflow handles a revised offer. Change one approved fact in the sample source and run the process again. Compare the new brief and draft with the previous versions. Check that the revision appears wherever it matters and that unrelated wording is not accidentally treated as a new claim. Keep the older approved version for reference if it remains relevant to previous work.

Use a consistent naming pattern for the results, such as the project, output type and review date. A reviewer should be able to identify the draft and open its source without searching through unrelated files.
